candidate.educational_objective: Apply the cited evidence to recognize the uniquely safest or most accurate nursing response in the clinical situation tested by V2-Q0123.

options.A: Any report by a healthcare worker automatically receives identical federal protection regardless of the applicable law, subject, reporting method, or context now.
options.B: A schedule change cannot qualify as retaliation because only termination or a reduction in salary is considered an adverse employment action.
options.C: The nurse must first resign before a retaliation complaint can be evaluated because continued employment prevents proof of an adverse action.
options.D: A reassignment may be retaliatory if it follows activity protected by an applicable whistleblower law; the specific protection depends on the governing statute.

candidate.rationale: OSHA explains that whistleblower protection depends on protected activity under an applicable law. Adverse actions can include reassignment, discipline, reduced hours, demotion, firing, or other actions that would deter a reasonable employee from raising concerns. Protection is therefore not automatic for every report; the relevant statute and facts matter.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Protected activities and retaliation standards vary by the specific whistleblower law; reassignment can be an adverse action.
candidate.source_locator: OSHA Whistleblower Protection Program FAQ — protected activity, adverse action including reassignment, and statute-specific coverage
candidate.stem: A nurse reports a safety concern to a regulatory agency and is then reassigned to undesirable shifts. Which statement best reflects federal whistleblower principles?
